newsitem.title: USA: Netanyahu says Mideast peace is two-way street.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu says Mideast peace is two-way street.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Monday Arabs must recognise that progress toward a Middle East peace is a two-way street requiring compromise from them as well as from Israel.
The right-wing Israeli leader, asked by reporters if he would stick to his insistence that the peace process must be "a two-way street," said, "Sure, everyone knows that already."

He commented at the start of day-long talks with President Bill Clinton and other U.S. leaders. Opening a meeting with Secretary of State Warren Christopher, Netanyahu said he would discuss ongoing talks with the Palestinians as well as "what we hope will be a resumption of talks with the Syrians."

He arrived early in the day for his second visit to Washington since he was elected in May, a development that put a further brake on Israel's already faltering peace process with Syria and the Palestinians.

His visit comes as events in Iraq have overshadowed, at least temporarily, the Israeli-Arab negotiations. But Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said on Sunday that Israel wanted to move ahead with peace talks with the Palestinians.
Netanyahu held a breakthrough meeting with Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat last Wednesday, an event that Washington pushed hard for and views as a way of giving momentum to the peace process.

The Iraqi crisis was also expected to figure prominently in Netanyahu's talks. Israel was the target of Iraqi Scud missile attacks during the 1991 Gulf War and Israelis flocked to gas mask distribution centres after U.S. forces launched missiles against southern Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Netanyahu was scheduled to meet Defence Secretary William Perry at 2:30 p.m. EDT (1830 GMT) before calling on Clinton at the White House at 4:40 p.m. EDT (2040 GMT).

Before a meeting in London with Levy on Sunday, Christopher pressed Israel for new "concrete steps" to advance Middle East peace after the Netanyahu-Arafat meeting, a theme that U.S. leaders were expected to take up on Monday.

Netanyahu has stalled on an Israeli promise to redeploy troops in the West Bank town of Hebron, saying he wants to alter the deal to safeguard better around 400 Jewish settlers living amidst 100,000 Palestinians in the heart of the city.

Palestinian and Israeli officials overseeing implementation of PLO-Israel peace deals met on Monday in the West Bank town of Jericho for the first time since Netanyahu's election, with Hebron at the top of the Palestinian agenda.

But talks between Israel and Syria have been deadlocked, with Damascus demanding that Netanyahu adopt the "land-for-peace" principle espoused by Israel's former Labour government and agree to withdraw from the Golan Heights.

Christopher said on Sunday that both Israel and Syria were interested in resuming talks, but State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns later said: "I cannot point to any recent progress in that area."
While Washington would like to see progress, few analysts expect any major U.S. initiative in the Middle East ahead of presidential elections Nov. 5.
Netanyahu said on Monday he would speak with Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole by phone. He met with Dole on his earlier visit to the United States in July.
The Israeli leader was to fly to New York on Monday evening for talks on Tuesday with U.S. business and Jewish leaders.
